submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a sharp, form-based retrospective detector of the Greek/Latin 'learned-name' word shape: it fires on the token that completes a word ending in a classical nominal suffix (-us, -a, -um, -is, -es, -os, -ia, -ium, -ius, -eus, -acus/-icus, -anus, -ensis, -ides, -ula, -acter, -illus), so it responds to ancient Greek/Roman names and places, to Latin biological names (Streptococcus, Bacillus, Candida, succinalis) and to invented words with the same endings, while the same stem with a vernacular ending (-am, -itz, -son, -ley, -stein, -ov, -ski) stays at zero. It is near zero for ordinary English words (including common Greek-derived vocabulary such as philosophy or democracy), for rare English words without that shape (flabbergasted, perspicacious), and for English/European family surnames and Anglo first names (Smith, Garcia, Schmidt, Rossi, Clinton, Kevin), while its output direction promotes further classical/foreign proper names (Herod, Hannibal, Hades, Assy, Philipp, Hussein, Saddam, Tayyip).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The county water authority released its annual report on Tuesday, and the document runs to more than two hundred pages. It describes repairs to eight pumping stations, the replacement of old lead service lines, and a new billing system that officials say will be simpler for residents to use. Demand fell slightly last year, the report notes, mostly because two large customers closed their plants and moved production to another state.

The first section covers the budget. Revenue came in about four percent above projections, thanks to a mild winter and lower than expected overtime for the maintenance crews. The board voted to put the surplus into a reserve fund for emergency repairs, though two members argued that some of it should go toward lowering rates for low income households. That debate is expected to continue at the next public meeting, which will be held at the community center.

Later chapters describe the condition of the pipes. Roughly a fifth of the system is more than sixty years old, and a map in the appendix shows where the oldest sections run under the downtown streets. Engineers recommend replacing them in stages over the next decade rather than all at once, because a single large project would require borrowing at current interest rates and would raise bills sharply for everyone. The report also lists the small leaks that were fixed during the year, along with the cost of each repair.

There is a short chapter on water quality. Samples are taken twice a week from twelve sites, and the results were within the limits set by the state in every case but one, when a sample from a dead end main showed slightly elevated levels of a mineral that is not considered harmful. The utility flushed that line and took new samples, which came back clean.

Among the items in the appendix is a brief history of the reservoir. It was surveyed in the nineteen twenties by a young engineer named Alcibiades Pappas, whose notebooks and hand drawn maps are still kept in a cabinet at the town library. The report reproduces one of his sketches, showing the original dam and the wooden footbridge that once crossed the spillway.

A separate chapter lists the road closures and detours planned for the summer, including a new sidewalk on Mill Street and a rebuilt culvert near the old grain elevator. Shop owners on the square have asked the council to postpone the work until after the harvest festival.

The final pages thank the crews who worked through the storm in March, and list the dates of the public hearings scheduled for the coming year. Residents who want a copy of the full document can request one at the front desk or download it from the authority's website.
